Name: Shrine of Shah Inayat Qadiri
Location: Mozang Chungi, Queens Road, Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
Founded/Opened: 18th century (c. 1728, per figure's death; a field survey separately gives 1141 AH)

Description:
## Overview

At Mozang Chungi on Queens Road, Lahore, not far from Fatima Jinnah Medical University, lies the shrine of Shah Inayat Qadiri — one of the most historically consequential Sufi figures of Mughal Punjab, not chiefly for his own writings, considerable though they were, but as the spiritual guide (*murshid*) of Bulleh Shah, arguably the most celebrated Punjabi Sufi poet of all.

## Life

Born around 1643 in Kasur into a farming family of the Arain community, Shah Inayat trained under a Shattari Sufi teacher — named in earlier sourcing for this entry as Muhammad Ali Raza Shattari, and named in a 2026 field survey as Hazrat Shah Raza Qadri Shattari; the two names are close but not identical, and neither source has been checked against the other here, so both are recorded rather than one being silently preferred. After friction with Kasur's ruling family — a 2026 field survey adds that local tradition attributes some of this friction to the ill intent of the ruler toward his wife, described as unusually beautiful and of noble family, though it frames this itself as a local account rather than settled fact — Shah Inayat migrated to Lahore, where he served as imam of the Oonchi Masjid near Bhati Gate and founded his own madrasa, teaching students without regard to caste or class. He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice and authored several Persian works of mystical philosophy, including the *Dastur-ul-Amal* (also independently named in the field survey) and *Lata'if-e-Ghaibiya*.

The field survey adds biographical detail not previously in this entry: his given name as Abul-Muarif Hanfi Qadri, his memorisation of the Qur'an by age five, and titles it records for him — Sheikh-ul-Mashaikh, Shah-e-Lahore, and Mufakkir-e-Pakistan.

## Bulleh Shah, Waris Shah, and His Wider Circle

His acceptance of Bulleh Shah as a disciple became one of the most retold episodes in Punjabi Sufi lore, precisely because it crossed rigid social boundaries: Bulleh Shah came from a Syed family of higher perceived status, yet sought out and remained devoted to a teacher of humbler, land-tilling background — facing, per the field survey, religious decrees (*fatwas*) from his own family over the choice, which he is recorded as answering only "what I have seen in him, you cannot perceive." This relationship, immortalised in Bulleh Shah's own verses, continues to be cited in Pakistan as an example of Sufism's disregard for caste hierarchy.

The field survey names Waris Shah as a second prominent disciple from this period, alongside Hazrat Hafiz Tabraiz, Maulana Jami, Deewan-e-Hafiz, and Deewan-e-Shams — without further detail on the nature of the latter connections.

## Family

Shah Inayat died around 1728 and is buried at Mozang alongside two of his sons, per existing sourcing for this entry. A 2026 field survey adds a daughter to the family (buried alongside him as well) and names the two sons: Zamanaullah, described as a Sufi poet who left no descendants, and Zahidullah, through whom the family line continued.

## The Shrine Today

His shrine, with its adjoining mosque, remains an active site of pilgrimage. The annual urs, observed 25-27 Jamadi al-Thani, draws thousands of devotees for nights of *zikr* and qawwali. A 2026 field survey adds detail on the shrine's ordinary devotional life: five daily prayers at the attached mosque, a weekly Mehfil-e-Milad with langar on Thursdays, and a corner set aside for lighting oil lamps, and gives visitor estimates of roughly 300-500 daily, rising to 1,500-3,000 on Thursday nights and 40,000-60,000 during the urs. Administration passed from the family's own descendants to the Auqaf Department, per the same survey.
